tr.td: Baisaran meadow, near Pahalgam, Anantnag district, Indian-administered Kashmir
26 civilians killed and more than a dozen injured; reports differ on whether the dead included a Nepali tourist or a local pony operator
The Resistance Front (TRF) claimed the attack and later retracted; India and its National Investigation Agency (NIA) blame Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba; Pakistan denies any involvement
Diplomatic reprisals, then a four-day India-Pakistan military confrontation from 7 to 10 May 2025; three men the NIA names as the attackers killed in July; NIA charge sheet filed in December 2025
Three men whom the NIA identifies as Pakistani nationals and members of Lashkar-e-Taiba; early Indian official estimates ranged from four to seven
About 2:23 p.m. according to the NIA charge sheet as reported by Daily Pioneer; an Indian official put it at about 2:45 p.m.
A manhunt; the NIA formally took over the case on 27 April 2025

Parvaiz Ahmad and Bashir Ahmad Jothar, arrested on 22 June 2025 for allegedly harbouring the attackers
28 July 2025, in an operation named Mahadev near Srinagar, according to the NIA and security forces

li.a: Al Jazeera: "Act of war", what happened in the Kashmir attack that killed 26 tourists
Al Jazeera: Kashmir attack, does India's Indus Waters Treaty freeze threaten Pakistan?
Al Jazeera: Operation Sindoor, what is the significance of India's Pakistan targets?
The Tribune: Indian Armed Forces launched Operation Sindoor, hitting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, says government
The Hindu: Ceasefire agreement struck, but Pakistan violates "understanding" along border
Deccan Herald: As India strikes Pakistan, a look at the status of the probe into the Pahalgam attack
Deccan Herald: Kashmir terror attack, NIA charges 7, names Pakistan LeT handler
Daily Pioneer: Pahalgam terror attack charge sheet, NIA details the Baisaran Valley plot

content.p: On the afternoon of 22 April 2025, armed men came out of a forest at Baisaran, a meadow above Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir that can only be reached on foot or by pony, and opened fire on tourists. At least 26 people were killed. Al Jazeera called it the deadliest attack of its kind in Indian-administered Kashmir in a quarter-century, and the Indian government blamed cross-border terrorism for it.

The attack was followed within days by tit-for-tat measures between India and Pakistan, then by a four-day military confrontation in May. Pakistan has denied any role, and India's NIA, in a charge sheet filed in December 2025, blames Pakistan-based operatives of Lashkar-e-Taiba. The case is now at the trial stage in Jammu. Each government's claims are set out below as that government made them.

Pahalgam was full of tourists in peak season. At about 2:45 p.m., an Indian official told Al Jazeera, a group of men in camouflage came out of the forest and fired indiscriminately. The NIA's charge sheet, as summarised by Daily Pioneer, puts the start of the assault at 2:23 p.m. Simran Chandani, a tourist from Nagpur, said she thought the sound was a balloon bursting before people rushed past. She said mostly men were fired upon. A tourist from Gujarat, Vinu Bai, 65, was treated in the district hospital for a bullet wound in the arm.

The dead were all men, Al Jazeera reported, and included a naval officer on his honeymoon, a retired banker, a realtor, an accountant and a Gulf returnee. Every account used here gives 26 dead, but the make-up differs. Al Jazeera and The Tribune wrote that 25 were Indian tourists and one was a Nepali national. Daily Pioneer, reporting the charge sheet, described 25 tourists and one local pony operator, and Deccan Herald 25 tourists and a local civilian. The NIA says the attackers asked victims to recite the Islamic declaration of faith and targeted non-Muslims, and that the pony operator died trying to disarm one of them.

Direct attacks on tourists have been rare in Kashmir even through three decades of armed rebellion, Al Jazeera noted. It listed earlier episodes, among them the 1995 abduction of six foreign tourists in Pahalgam by the Al-Faran group, a 2000 attack at Nunwan in Pahalgam that killed 32 people, including 21 Hindu pilgrims, and the 2017 shooting of eight pilgrims in Anantnag. The 22 April attack happened while US Vice President JD Vance was visiting India, and Modi cut short a trip to Saudi Arabia to return. Iltija Mufti, a local politician, said the area was usually patrolled heavily by security forces and called the attack "extremely shocking". After the killings, Deccan Herald reported, tourist bookings across south Kashmir were cancelled en masse and armed presence at tourist spots grew.

A statement in the name of The Resistance Front (TRF) claimed responsibility. It tied the attack to the residency permits issued to non-Kashmiris after India stripped the region of its semi-autonomous status in 2019, according to Al Jazeera, which could not confirm that the statement was authentic. Indian authorities say TRF is a front for Lashkar-e-Taiba. The Daily Pioneer reported that TRF later retracted its claim. On 17 July the US State Department designated TRF a Foreign Terrorist Organization, saying it had claimed responsibility for the attack, which it called the deadliest on civilians in India since the 2008 Mumbai attacks.

On 23 April, after a meeting led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India's foreign secretary, Vikram Misri, said that the cross-border linkages of the attack had been put to the cabinet's security committee, and that the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 would be "held in abeyance with immediate effect until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism". India also closed the Attari-Wagah crossing and cancelled the SAARC visa-exemption visas held by Pakistanis. The next day Modi promised that India would find, follow and punish every "terrorist" and those who back them.

Pakistan answered with similar steps and threatened to suspend all bilateral agreements, including the 1972 Simla Agreement. It said any disruption of its water would be "an act of war". Pakistan denied involvement and called for a neutral investigation, Al Jazeera reported. Pakistani lawyer Ahmer Bilal Soofi told Al Jazeera that the treaty has no provision for holding it in abeyance. Pakistan says the Indus basin irrigates about 80 percent of its arid land, NPR reported. NPR reported that India's Home Minister, Amit Shah, vowed to "never" restore the treaty, and that late in June a treaty-mandated arbitration tribunal said it kept jurisdiction over a dispute despite India's position, which India rejected.

In the early hours of 7 May India launched what it called Operation Sindoor. India's Ministry of Defence said it struck nine sites of "terrorist infrastructure" in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir and that no Pakistani military facilities were hit. At a briefing, Misri said the strikes focused on dismantling terrorist infrastructure and disabling terrorists likely to be sent into India, and military officers said five of the nine sites were in Pakistan-administered Kashmir and four in Punjab.

Pakistan's military spokesman, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, called it an "unprovoked attack, targeting innocent people". He said at least 31 civilians had died across six locations, including women and children, and that mosques and residential areas were hit. Pakistan's military also claimed to have shot down several Indian military aircraft. Al Jazeera said it could not independently verify the claims of either army. The Deccan Herald described the confrontation as lasting from 7 to 10 May, with cross-border firing, drone activity and precision strikes.

On 10 May India's External Affairs Minister, S Jaishankar, announced an "understanding" to stop military action and firing after three days of intense hostilities. Indian official sources said it had been agreed bilaterally and would not affect India's punitive measures. NPR reported it as a ceasefire negotiated by the United States. The Hindu's headline the same day said Pakistan had violated the understanding along the border.

The NIA formally took over the case on 27 April. On 7 May, the day of the strikes, the agency said that Sheikh Sajjad Gul, the TRF head, was the mastermind, and that communications had been traced to him, Deccan Herald reported. The December charge sheet instead named a Pakistan-based Lashkar handler, Sajid Jatt, as the conspirator who coordinated the attack through Lashkar and TRF.

On 22 June the NIA arrested two Pahalgam residents, Parvaiz Ahmad and Bashir Ahmad Jothar, for harbouring the attackers. According to the charge sheet, the attackers sought food and shelter with them the night before and asked about security and the upcoming Amarnath Yatra, and the two were paid. They are accused, and the case is at the trial stage. On 28 July security forces killed three men in an operation called Mahadev in the Dachigam forest. The NIA names them as Faisal Jatt, who also used the name Suleman Shah, Habeeb Tahir, known as Jibran, and Hamza Afghani.

The 1,597-page charge sheet of 15 December names seven accused, among them LeT and TRF as legal entities, Sajid Jatt and the three dead men. It invokes the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Arms Act. The NIA says phones traced to Lahore and Karachi, Pakistani voter identity documents and other items point to cross-border involvement. Home Minister Shah later told Parliament that the involvement of Pakistan-based Lashkar operatives had been established, while Pakistan denies any role.
